title: India Just Launched a Fuel That Costs ₹20 Less Per Litre. Your Car Cannot Use It.
excerpt: E85, an 85 percent ethanol blend, went live at 48 stations on World Environment Day. But only flex-fuel vehicles — a tiny fraction of India's fleet — can fill up.
body:
India Just Launched a Fuel That Costs ₹20 Less Per Litre. Your Car Cannot Use It.
=============================

India has formally entered the high-ethanol fuel era. On World Environment Day, June 5, Union Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri inaugurated the country's first E85 fuel dispensing station at an Indian Oil outlet on Pusa Road in New Delhi — a blend of 85 percent ethanol and 15 percent petrol, priced at ₹82.12 per litre, roughly ₹20 cheaper than the standard E20 petrol most Indians pump today.

The launch is not a pilot. Forty-eight public sector fuel stations across the country were switched on the same day, with plans to scale to 500 outlets by December 2026 and approximately 5,000 by the end of 2027. But there is a catch that will define whether this is a real transition or a symbolic one: E85 cannot be used in existing petrol vehicles. It is designed exclusively for flex-fuel vehicles, or FFVs, whose engines are built to run on ethanol blends ranging from E20 to E100.

x-official:https://x.com/HardeepSPuri/status/2063080493034488232

## The Vehicles Are Already Here

Maruti Suzuki has rolled out a flex-fuel variant of its best-selling WagonR. Hero MotoCorp has launched a flex-fuel Splendor. More models are expected in the coming months, though Puri was careful to note that the government is not mandating automakers to produce FFVs. "The transition will depend on rigorous testing by automobile manufacturers," he said. The government is also considering distinct number plates for E85-compliant vehicles, a move that echoes Brazil's early-stage labelling system when it launched flex-fuel decades ago.

The comparison to Brazil is instructive and humbling. In South America's largest economy, flex-fuel adoption is near-universal, and the price gap between ethanol and conventional fuel runs closer to 36 percent. India's current delta is under 20 percent. Factor in that E85 delivers roughly 25 to 35 percent lower mileage than E20 — ethanol simply carries less energy per litre than petrol — and the real-world cost savings for early adopters will be thin.

## The Bigger Picture: ₹1.84 Lakh Crore Saved

The economics make more sense at the national level than at the pump. India imports about 60 percent of its LPG and is the world's third-largest oil importer, spending roughly $120 billion annually on crude. The ethanol blending programme, which Puri described as "five years ahead of schedule," has already lifted the national average from 1.53 percent blending in 2014 to 20 percent today. That trajectory alone has saved over ₹1.84 lakh crore in foreign exchange and reduced crude imports by nearly 302 lakh metric tonnes.

The E85 rollout is designed to push aggregate blending to 26 percent by 2030-31. For sugar cane farmers and grain producers in Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Karnataka — the backbone of India's ethanol supply chain — higher blending means guaranteed procurement at remunerative prices. The government has positioned this as a farmer-income story as much as an energy-security one.

## What It Means for NRIs

For diaspora families who send money home or invest in rural India, the ethanol economy is a structural shift worth watching. Ethanol distilleries have become one of the fastest-growing rural industrial assets in India, and the expansion of FFV infrastructure could ripple through sugar cooperatives, agri-tech startups, and the broader farm-to-fuel supply chain that touches millions of households. This shift not only supports local economies but also has implications for remittances, as increased agricultural productivity can lead to higher incomes for families reliant on these funds.

Moreover, as the Indian government looks to enhance energy security through domestic production, NRIs with ties to India may find new opportunities in sustainable investments and green technology sectors. The potential for dual citizenship holders to engage in these emerging markets could further strengthen family ties and economic connections across borders. For instance, NRIs might consider investing in ethanol production facilities or supporting agri-tech innovations that optimize the supply chain, thereby directly contributing to India's energy independence.

India's oil secretary, Neeraj Mittal, separately announced that the government is working on a programme to boost compressed biogas production — another signal that New Delhi is building out a diversified energy stack rather than betting on a single alternative.

The question is speed. At 48 stations out of 90,000 nationwide, E85 is less than a rounding error today. Whether it becomes Brazil or remains a policy brochure depends entirely on how fast automakers move and how aggressively the government expands distribution. The fuel is ready. The ecosystem is not — yet.

*Sources: Reuters, Livemint, Outlook Business, Dainik Bhaskar*
